coverageDimensions:
RESOURCE TYPE coverage is the only one this page actually supplies, and it supplies it cleanly. It means: of the AWS resource types that can carry a resource-based policy or a sharing ACL, how many can this analyzer read? The page gives 15 for external access, 6 for internal access, 2 for unused access, each hand-counted off a list. For internal access it even supplies its own local denominator, since the external list is the superset it is measured against — 6 of 15, with the 9 gaps named. The full-AWS denominator has to come from elsewhere; the page only gives you the numerator and the names.

SERVICE coverage would mean: of all AWS services, how many does this analyzer reach at all? The page gives you nothing directly. You can derive a service list by rolling the resource types up — S3, IAM, KMS, Lambda, SQS, Secrets Manager, SNS, EBS, RDS, ECR, EFS, DynamoDB, which is 12 services across the 15 external types (S3 contributes 2 types, RDS 2, DynamoDB 2) — but that derivation is misleading and I would not present it as service coverage. "S3 is covered" would be read as the whole service, when what is covered is buckets and directory buckets, explicitly not cross-account access point policies. "RDS is covered" would be read as databases, when the page says in a Note that access configured directly on the database is NOT identified — only snapshots and cluster snapshots are. A service rollup here converts a precise claim into a false one. The page publishes resource types; measure resource types.

REGION coverage would mean: in which AWS Regions can each analyzer type run? The page gives you nothing usable. It asserts a Region dimension exists — analysis is scoped to "the Region where you enabled IAM Access Analyzer", and an IAM role is global so a finding is raised "in each enabled Region" — but it never names a single Region and never enumerates enabled Regions. There is no Region axis to extract here. Any Region coverage claim must come from a different page.

features.featureName: IAM Access Analyzer supported resource types for external access
features.reasoning: This is a standalone capability because it has its own list, distinct from the internal-access list. The values are AWS resource types — a universe that exists independently of IAM Access Analyzer, so a ratio against the full set of AWS resource types is a genuine coverage measure. Note "AWS Lambda functions and layers" is ONE list entry with one section, not two; "DynamoDB streams" and "DynamoDB tables" are two separate entries with two separate sections; "S3 buckets" and "S3 directory buckets" are likewise two. Anything finer than the entry (aliases, versions, access points, indexes) is prose detail, not a value.
features.scope: Per analyzer type (external access analyzer). Secondary Region dimension is asserted but not enumerated: analysis covers resources "in the Region where you enabled IAM Access Analyzer", and an IAM role, being global, "generates a finding in each enabled Region".
features.statuses: 15 of 15 stated as supported. Counted off the bullet list under "Supported resource types for external access": S3 buckets; S3 directory buckets; IAM roles; KMS keys; Lambda functions and layers; SQS queues; Secrets Manager secrets; SNS topics; EBS volume snapshots; RDS DB snapshots; RDS DB cluster snapshots; ECR repositories; EFS file systems; DynamoDB streams; DynamoDB tables. Each has a matching H2 section, so the list and the sections cross-check at 15. No resource type is listed here as not supported — there is no Yes/No column and no retired/deprecated marking anywhere on the page. The page does state sub-resource exclusions inside supported types, and these are NOT axis values: Lambda aliases and specific versions invoked by qualified ARN are not reported (functions and layers are); cross-account access point policies are not analyzed for S3 general purpose and directory buckets; for RDS, access configured directly on the database itself is not identified, and RAM shares of DB clusters and clones are not monitored. Treat those as scope narrowing on an existing covered type, not as separate not-covered entries.

features.featureName: IAM Access Analyzer supported resource types for internal access
features.reasoning: A different list means a different capability. The internal-access list is a strict subset of the external one, so folding the two together would silently claim internal coverage for nine types the page denies. The axis is still AWS resource types, still external, so the ratio is meaningful — and here the page hands you both the numerator and an explicit denominator.
features.scope: Per analyzer type (internal access analyzer). Same unenumerated per-Region dimension as external access.
features.statuses: 6 stated as supported, counted off the bullet list under "Supported resource types for internal access": S3 buckets; S3 directory buckets; RDS DB snapshots; RDS DB cluster snapshots; DynamoDB streams; DynamoDB tables. 9 stated as NOT supported, and the page states this two ways rather than in a column. First in prose in the opening Note: "Internal access analyzers don't support all resource types that external access analyzers support." Second by omission from the list, which the Note licenses you to read as exclusion: IAM roles, KMS keys, Lambda functions and layers, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets, SNS topics, EBS volume snapshots, ECR repositories, EFS file systems — 9 types, 15 minus 6. The six supported types are each confirmed a second time inside their own H2 section by a sentence beginning "For internal access analyzers, IAM Access Analyzer generates a finding when a principal (user or role) within your organization or account has access to...". The nine unsupported types have no such sentence in their sections. That is the page's real Yes/No signal and it agrees with the list exactly.

features.featureName: Unused access analyzer supported resource types
features.reasoning: This is a third, separately enumerable capability that a reader would miss because it has no heading and no section — it lives only inside a Note. It belongs in the map because it is exactly the shape of a coverage claim: a named capability, an enumerable set, and an explicit boundary word ("only"). Do not merge it into external or internal access; unused access analyzers examine IAM usage, not resource-based policies, and the page's own framing keeps the three analyzer types apart.
features.scope: Per analyzer type (unused access analyzer). No Region detail given for this analyzer type on this page.
features.statuses: 2 stated as supported: IAM users and IAM roles. The whole claim is one sentence in the opening Note: "Unused access analyzers only support IAM users and roles." The word "only" is an explicit exclusion of everything else, so the other 14 external-access types (all 15 except IAM roles) are stated as not supported for unused access. Note that IAM users appear nowhere else on the page — this is the only mention, and there is no H2 section for them. Low-detail claim: take it, but record that its source is a single prose sentence, not a list or a table.

pageTitle: IAM Access Analyzer supported resource types for external and internal access
shouldNotExtract: The "See also" block at the foot is AWS's new boilerplate about skills for AI coding assistants, including the `aws agent-toolkit search-skills` command and the Agent Toolkit link — drop the whole block. Drop all four code blocks in the KMS section: the two example policy statements and the ACCESS_DENIED finding JSON. That finding JSON contains `"resourceType": "AWS::KMS::Key"` and an ARN, and both are examples, not enumerated values. Drop the KMS Access Denied troubleshooting narrative (what the error looks like, the fix policy to apply, the move to Resolved status). Drop the timing figures: the 6-hour account-level Block Public Access evaluation, the 6-hour multi-Region access point evaluation, and the 24-hour periodic rescan — these are scan cadence, not coverage. Drop the RDS sharing limits ("up to 20 other accounts", encrypted snapshots cannot be public) — those are RDS behaviour and quota, not IAM Access Analyzer coverage. Drop condition keys, attributes and API names used as explanatory detail: kms:CallerAccount, ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, CreateVolumePermissions, AddPermission, "Everyone". Drop all cross-references and outbound links (Block Public Access, create a filter, trust policies, Working with directory buckets, DynamoDB IAM actions, Creating a DB snapshot, Understand how IAM Access Analyzer findings work), and drop the `<a name="...">` anchors and the in-page `#access-analyzer-*` link targets — the anchors are markup, not values.
trap:
The obvious trap is flattening the two bullet lists into one. The lists share entries and share anchor targets — six of the internal entries point at the exact same `#access-analyzer-s3`, `#access-analyzer-rds-db`, `#access-analyzer-ddb-table` anchors as the external ones. A parser that dedupes by anchor or by link text produces a single 15-item list and silently claims internal-access coverage for KMS, Lambda, SQS, SNS, EBS, ECR, EFS and IAM roles, all of which the page excludes. A parser that does not dedupe reports 21 resource types, which is also wrong.

The mirror-image trap is keying on H2 sections instead of the lists. There are 15 per-type sections and they mirror the EXTERNAL list only. Internal access has no sections of its own, so a section-driven parser reports internal-access coverage as zero or missing, when the page in fact states it precisely — and states it twice, once in the list and once in the "For internal access analyzers..." sentence inside six of the sections.

Third: the unused access analyzer claim is invisible to anything that reads headings and lists. It exists solely as the sentence "Unused access analyzers only support IAM users and roles" inside a Note, and it is the only place IAM users are mentioned on the page at all.

Fourth: promoting sub-resource prose into axis values. "Functions, versions, aliases, and layers", access points, multi-Region access points, DynamoDB indexes, and "DB clusters and clones" all read like resource types in isolation. They are qualifiers on a covered type or exclusions within it. Turning "aliases" and "versions" into two unsupported resource types inflates both numerator and denominator with things AWS never listed. Relatedly, "AWS Lambda functions and layers" is one entry — splitting it into two makes the external count 16.

Fifth: reading the per-type caveats as not-covered rows. Cross-account access point policies, direct database access, and RAM shares of DB clusters are stated exclusions, but they are not values on the resource-type axis, so they do not belong in a covered/not-covered tally. Record them as scope notes on the type or lose them.
whatThePageStates: The page tells you which AWS resource types IAM Access Analyzer can analyze, and it splits that answer by analyzer type. It first gives two explicit bullet lists — "Supported resource types for external access" (15 entries) and "Supported resource types for internal access" (6 entries) — and a Note that adds a third, smaller list: "Unused access analyzers only support IAM users and roles." The rest of the page is one H2 section per external-access resource type (15 sections) that explains what policy or sharing mechanism is read for that type, plus per-type caveats about what is deliberately not analyzed. The unit of the page is the resource type; the page analyses only resource-based policies (and, for EBS/RDS snapshots, sharing ACLs), in the Region where the analyzer is enabled.
